analysis.one_liner: Exempts legally applied pesticides from Clean Water Act discharge permits.
analysis.headline: The bill won bipartisan committee approval with 21 Senate cosponsors and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 2011 federal appeals court ruling, spraying EPA-approved pesticides into or near streams, canals, and lakes requires a Clean Water Act permit, just like other pipe discharges. This bill would change both the pesticide law and the Clean Water Act to say that a permit is not required when the pesticide and its residue were applied legally under the pesticide law. Permits would still be needed for misuse of a pesticide, for regulated stormwater, and for industrial wastewater and vessel discharges. It would also require the EPA to report on how well pesticide registration protects water quality.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, forestry operators, irrigation districts, mosquito-control districts, pesticide applicators, and anyone else who sprays pesticides in or near water. They would no longer need federal discharge permits, with their fees, paperwork, monitoring, and public notice, for routine, lawful pesticide applications.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids the EPA or any state from requiring a Clean Water Act permit for a discharge of a pesticide that is authorized for sale and use under the pesticide law, or its residue, when applied lawfully.

Permits would still be required for pesticide applications that violate water-quality-related provisions of the pesticide law, for regulated stormwater, and for industrial and vessel discharges containing pesticides.

The bill directs the EPA, with the Agriculture Department, to report within a year on coordination between its water and pesticide offices, on how well pesticide regulation protects water quality, and on how the pesticide law could be changed to better protect water quality and health.

analysis.who_pays: People who fish, swim, drink, or draw livelihoods from waters receiving pesticide runoff would lose a layer of oversight: the permit process that sets conditions on each application, triggers monitoring, and creates a public record of what is discharged. Responsibility for water harm would shift to proving a pesticide-law violation after the fact.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities relying on waters near spraying

drawbacks.text: Removing the permit requirement eliminates site-specific conditions, monitoring, public notice, and enforcement triggers under the Clean Water Act, leaving water-quality protection for pesticide sprays to the pesticide law's general registration process and after-the-fact violation cases.

Under the bill, a permit could only be demanded when a discharge resulted from a pesticide-law violation, so regulators would have to prove wrongdoing before they could impose water-quality conditions on repeated sprays into the same waters.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that requiring permits for lawful pesticide use duplicates rules the pesticide law already imposes through product labels, and that it burdens farmers, mosquito-control agencies, and irrigation districts for ordinary, approved applications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost savings for applicators are real, since the 2011 court ruling did impose a permitting layer on top of the pesticide-law label system. But that permit layer is where water-specific limits, monitoring, and public accountability live; the bill would replace it with general pesticide registration plus enforcement only after a violation is proven. Communities downstream bear the difference, and the one-year EPA study the bill orders comes only after the permit requirement is already gone.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in June 2015 by Senator Crapo with 15 original cosponsors and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
In August 2015 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment, and on October 29, 2015 it was reported by Chairman Inhofe with written report No. 114-160.

The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 284, the list of bills awaiting floor action; minority views were filed in the committee report.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing requirement that pesticide sprays into or near waters carry a Clean Water Act permit stayed in place, so downstream communities and water-quality oversight came out ahead. Pesticide users gained nothing new but also faced no further change.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan on paper (16 of 54 Republicans and 5 of 44 Democrats as cosponsors), but the committee's report carried minority views from the Democratic side and the bill never came to a floor vote, so no recorded vote shows the chamber's split.

industries.industry: Agriculture, forestry, irrigation, and mosquito-control applicators
industries.note: These are the users who spray pesticides into or near water and would be freed from Clean Water Act permits, fees, monitoring, and public notice. Their gain comes at the cost of downstream oversight of what enters shared waters.
With permits no longer required for lawful use, the product label would be the main water-quality check, reducing a compliance layer that documents and constrains discharges of their products.

industries.industry: Clean-water monitoring, permitting, and environmental services
industries.note: Firms and agencies that prepare NPDES pesticide permits and run associated monitoring would lose that work if the permit requirement were repealed for lawful pesticide applications.
